latestPost.title: Jeonse and Interest Rates: How Did Seoul Apartment Jeonse Prices Move Relative to the Policy Rate and Loan Rates, and With What Lag? (2003.11–2026.10)
latestPost.body:
Data as of 2026.11.19 | Seoul apartment jeonse price index (monthly), base rate, and deposit-bank mortgage and jeonse-loan rates (new-business basis)

Sources: the jeonse price index is from the Korea Real Estate Board (formerly the Korea Appraisal Board), and interest rates are from the Bank of Korea ECOS. Unless noted otherwise, all data in this post come from these two sources.

Key Takeaways

  • 22 years at a glance. The Seoul apartment jeonse index rose 2.20x between 2003.11 and 2026.10 (3.5% per year on average). The peak was 2022.01 (104.29) and the trough 2023.05 (84.08), a 19.4% decline. As of 2026.10 the index is -0.4% from the peak and +10.5% year over year.

  • Same-period correlations flip sign across sub-periods. The correlation between jeonse YoY and the 12-month change in the base rate is +0.69 for 2004–2012, -0.51 for 2013–2019 and -0.60 for 2020–2026.09, yet it is -0.04 (effectively zero) for the full sample.

  • With lags, rates lead from 2013 onward. In quarterly changes, when the base rate leads by 1~2 quarters the correlation falls to between -0.57 and -0.70. The pattern looks like jeonse growth slowing 3~6 months after rates rise. In the 60-month rolling correlation, 88% of the 117 windows ending 2016.12 or later show this pattern, versus 1% of the 72 earlier windows.

  • Before 2012 it is the opposite. Jeonse also rose during the 2005–08 and 2010–11 hiking cycles (annualized +6.8% and +10.6%), and the sum of the rate coefficients in the distributed-lag regression is +1.64 (positive).

  • Granger tests show that the base rate predicts jeonse, but jeonse does not predict the base rate (p≤0.001 versus 0.08~0.61 from 2013 onward). Mortgage and jeonse-loan rates run in both directions, so they mix in market reactions.

  • However, robustness is weak. Excluding the 2021.8–2023.1 hiking cycle (2021Q3–2023Q4), the base-rate coefficient sum for 2013 onward falls from -7.62 to -4.25 (p=0.062), and the mortgage-rate coefficient sum from -7.29 to -1.56 (p=0.40). A single hiking cycle, 2022–23, drives much of the result, and there are only two or three independent hiking cycles in the sample.

  • 2026 so far. The base rate rose to 2.75% in July and 3.00% in August, yet jeonse is still rising at +10.5% YoY. The monthly gain has slowed from +1.37% in June to +0.76% in October. The mortgage rate was nearly flat from 4.29% to 4.36% over January–June, then began rising in July and reached 4.88% in September (the base-rate hikes started in July). If past patterns hold, the effect could show up with a delay, but this is an observation point, not a forecast.

  • Regional split. Gangnam’s three districts, the rest of southern Seoul and northern Seoul all responded to rates in the same direction (Σβ -8.65, -7.81, -6.92), and their peak-to-trough declines were similar (-20.2%, -20.2%, -18.6%). As of 2026.10, only northern Seoul has recovered to its peak.

  • Is it a monetary phenomenon? In the earlier post, M2 did not consistently lead jeonse. In this analysis, a leading relationship appears from 2013 onward with the “price of money”, the interest rate, rather than the quantity of money, but the sample and controls are too limited to read it as causal. The next task is to put supply of new completions, regulation and M2 into one model and see whether the rate effect survives.

Jeonse: a Korean lease system in which the tenant pays a large, refundable lump-sum deposit to the landlord instead of monthly rent. The deposit is returned when the lease ends.

Jeonse index and base period: a number that sets the price at a base date to 100 and shows how much prices have risen since. This post sets 2026.06 to 100, so 103.84 means 3.84% higher than 2026.06.

YoY (year over year): the percentage change from 12 months earlier. Comparing the same months removes seasonal effects. A jeonse YoY of +10.5% means prices are up 10.5% from a year ago.

%p (percentage point): the difference between two values that are already percentages, such as interest rates. A base rate moving from 2.50% to 3.00% is a 0.5%p rise, not a 20% rise.

Lag and lead: a relationship in which one variable moves first and the other responds some months later. “The rate leads by 2 quarters” means the rate moved first and jeonse reacted two quarters later.

Correlation coefficient (r): a number between -1 and +1 showing how closely two values move together. Plus means the same direction, minus the opposite direction, and near 0 a weak relationship. An absolute value of 0.7 or more is generally strong. It does not prove cause and effect.

Cross-correlation: shifting the lag one quarter at a time and computing the correlation each time, to find the lag at which the relationship is strongest.

Significance threshold (|r|≥0.37, etc.): with small samples, a large correlation can appear by chance, so correlations smaller than this value cannot be distinguished from chance. With 28 quarters the threshold is 0.37.

Rolling correlation: recomputing the correlation while sliding a 60-month window forward one month at a time, to see whether the relationship changes over time.

Stationarity (ADF test): a check of whether the mean and variability of a series stay roughly stable over time. If not, spurious correlations arise easily, so the series is converted to rates of change before testing.

Granger test: a test of whether knowing past rate changes helps predict the next jeonse change. It looks only at “does it help predict” and does not prove true causation. The reverse direction (whether jeonse predicts rates) is checked as well.

p-value: the probability of seeing a result this strong by chance if there were truly no relationship. Below 0.05 is conventionally taken to mean it is hard to attribute to chance. A 0.000 in a table means it is close to zero to three decimal places.

Distributed-lag regression and Σβ: estimates the effect of a rate change on jeonse growth over several subsequent quarters at once, and Σβ is the sum of those effects. A Σβ of -7.62 means that after a 1%p rate rise, jeonse growth is lower by about 7.6%p in total over five quarters. Likewise, it does not assert causation.

t-value and R²: the t-value shows how far the relationship is from zero, and an absolute value of 2 or more is read as not due to chance. R² is the share of the variation in jeonse that the model explains. 0.54 means 54%.

HAC (Newey-West) standard errors: correct for the clustering of errors that arises because consecutive quarters are similar, so the results do not look more certain than they are.

Annualization: converting changes over periods of different lengths to a one-year basis. +4% over 4 months is roughly 12~13% per year. Short periods can be exaggerated, which is why Section 3 calls them “for reference only”.

Event study: overlaying the jeonse path before and after the month a rate hiking cycle began.

New-business-basis rates and provisional figures: new-business-basis rates are the rates on newly extended loans, so they react to market changes faster than rates on the existing loan balance. Provisional figures may be revised later.

1. Data and Method

1-1. Data Used

Variable | Source | Period | Unit | Notes
Seoul apartment jeonse price index | Seoul apartment jeonse price index (monthly) | 2003.11–2026.10 (276 months) | 2026.06=100 | Seoul overall and 25 districts
Base rate | ECOS 1.3.1 | 1999.05–2026.10 | % per year | Monthly values
Mortgage rate | ECOS 1.3.3.2.1 Deposit-bank lending rates (new-business basis) | 2001.09–2026.09 | % per year | Monthly values. 2026.09 is provisional
Jeonse-loan rate | Same table as above | 2015.01–2026.09 (141 months) | % per year | Monthly values. 2026.09 is provisional

The same ECOS lending-rate table also has guaranteed loans and fixed-rate and floating-rate mortgages (from 2013.01), but they are not used in the main text. The analysis period runs through 2026.09, when the loan rates end, and the 2026.10 values are included only in the descriptive statistics.

1-2. Variable Definitions

  • Jeonse YoY: percentage change of the index from 12 months earlier.

  • Jeonse quarterly change: log difference of the quarter-end index ×100. Because each quarter’s change is independent, the overlap problem is smaller than with monthly YoY.

  • Rate change: the 12-month change is the %p difference from 12 months earlier, and the quarterly change is the %p difference in the quarter-end rate.

  • Lag k: the rate is placed k periods ahead of jeonse for comparison. Positive k means the rate leads, and negative k means jeonse leads. A negative correlation means that jeonse growth slows after the rate rises.

  • Significance threshold: for sample size n, roughly |r|≥1.96/√n is distinguishable from 0 at the 5% level (0.37 when n=28).

2. 22 Years at a Glance: Jeonse and Rates Side by Side

The overall picture is as follows. The Seoul jeonse index grew 2.20x, from 47.10 in 2003.11 to 103.84 in 2026.10. Jeonse rose sharply during the 2012.7–2016.6 rate-cut period and the 2019.7–2021.7 low-rate period, then fell -10.1% in 2022, when the base rate rose 2.25%p, and -6.9% in 2023. On the other hand, rates also rose in 2005–2008 and 2010–2011, but jeonse rose +6~13% per year. In other words, the direction of rates alone did not determine the direction of jeonse.

The mortgage rate fell from 7.00% (annual average) in 2008 to 2.91% in 2016, rose again to 4.37% in 2023, and averages 4.44% for January–September 2026. The jeonse-loan rate moved together with the mortgage rate within ±0.33%p on an annual-average basis.

3. Jeonse by Rate Phase

The periods are split into hiking, cutting and holding phases based on when the base rate changed, and the annualized change in Seoul jeonse is calculated for each phase. The last column is the same calculation for a window of equal length shifted six months later, to gauge whether the effect shows up with a delay.

How to read this and how to interpret it:

  • Before 2016, jeonse rose during hiking periods. From 2005.10 to 2008.8 it was +6.8% annualized, and from 2010.7 to 2011.6 it was +10.6%. This appears to be the continuation of the rising jeonse trend that preceded the hikes, and it is consistent with the earlier post’s explanation that jeonse in this period depended heavily on supply factors such as new completions and redevelopment relocations (this data does not confirm it).

  • After 2016, jeonse slowed or fell during hiking periods. In 2017.11–2018.11 it was +0.6% in the same period, then turned to -2.1% in the window six months later. In 2021.8–2023.1 it was -8.0% in the same period and fell more sharply to -13.1% in the shifted window. In both cases the later window looks worse. This can be read as the rate effect arriving with a delay.

  • Cutting periods are not uniform either. 2008.9–2009.2 was -10.7% (the financial crisis coinciding with move-ins to large complexes in Jamsil), 2012.7–2016.6 was +7.0%, and 2019.7–2020.5 was +3.3% (+5.0% in the shifted window).

  • The four months since 2026.7 show +12.0% annualized in the same period, so jeonse is still rising. The window is too short, so treat this as reference only.

  • Phases are split by the timing of rate changes, so their lengths vary from 4 to 48 months. Directly comparing annualized values over periods of different lengths can exaggerate the shorter ones.

4. Lag Analysis ①: Cross-Correlation of Quarterly Changes

4-5. How to Read These Results

  • 2004–2012: the same-quarter correlation is +0.60, and the case where jeonse leads by one quarter (-1) is also +0.39. Jeonse did not slow after rates rose; rates rose along with jeonse during periods when jeonse was rising. The Bank of Korea may have reacted to an overheating market, or a common economic factor may have moved both (hypothesis).

  • The two sub-periods from 2013 onward: when the rate leads by 1~2 quarters, the correlation is -0.57~-0.70, exceeding the threshold (0.37~0.38). It remains significant through 3 quarters (-0.42~-0.45) and disappears by about 6 quarters. It is notable that the two sub-periods have a similar shape.

  • The mortgage rate is weaker than the base rate at a 2-quarter lead after 2020 (-0.50), and slower at a 3~5 quarter lead in 2013–2019 (-0.39~-0.52). Loan rates are affected by spreads and regulation, so the signal is blurrier than for the base rate.

  • The jeonse-loan rate is -0.55 at a 1-quarter lead. The +0.42 when jeonse moves first (-1) suggests that a response in which jeonse-loan rates rise after jeonse rises may be mixed in.

  • The full-sample correlation (around -0.30) is smaller than the sub-period values because the opposite signs of 2004–2012 are mixed in.

5. Lag Analysis ②: Monthly YoY Cross-Correlation and 60-Month Rolling
